raw_response:
I'm 68 this year, and I've been working these same 5 mu in Quzhou for 50 years. My father farmed here before me, and I know where the soil is heavy and where it drains fast. I finished middle school—back then that meant something in the village—so I can read the fertilizer bags and I've been to a few extension meetings. But honestly, most of what I trust comes from doing it myself and watching my neighbors. If Lao Wang down the lane tries something new and it works, I pay attention. If it fails, I stick to my old ways.

My household has seven people, but my son and daughter-in-law work over in Handan at a factory. My younger daughter is married out. That leaves me, my wife, my grandson who's in middle school, and my elderly mother-in-law at home. The boy helps on weekends but he's got homework. So mostly it's me and the old woman in the fields. We can't hire labor for daily work—where would the money come from? My son sends back maybe 20,000 yuan a year, which covers the big expenses, but the farm has to pay for itself. I always keep a few hundred yuan cash in the drawer for mother's medicine, so I don't throw everything into the fields.

For the wheat, I planted it last October like always—around the 8th, after the National Day holiday when my son was home to help turn the soil. I used the same improved semi-dwarf variety as the past three years. It doesn't lodge in wind and the flour tastes familiar. For base fertilizer I spread about 40 kg per mu of 15-15-15 compound fertilizer and about 10 kg of urea before sowing. The extension agent says I should use 18 kg nitrogen per mu total, but I've always done about 14 kg and gotten stable yields. I'm not made of money. Last year Lao Wang put on 20 kg N and only got maybe 50 jin more per mu than me—at today's prices that's not worth the extra 40 yuan per mu. I'd rather apply a little too much than too little, because a bad year hurts more than a good year helps, but 14 kg is my safe spot.

Now it's April and the wheat is at jointing stage, looking greener than last year because we had good winter snow. I'll topdress another 15 kg of urea per mu this week. I'll irrigate three times: now at jointing, once at heading in mid-May, and once during grain filling if June turns dry. Each pumping costs about 25 yuan in electricity for the whole 5 mu, so if rain comes I skip it—water is money. For weeds, I already sprayed herbicide once in early March. That's enough if you time it right. We harvest around June 8th–10th with the combine. I pay 50 yuan per mu—250 yuan total—but at my age I can't swing a sickle across 5 mu anymore. My son takes a week off then; it's the only time he can help.

The maize has to go in within five days of wheat harvest, sometimes three days if the weather turns hot. We shred the wheat straw, spread it, and plant directly with our small hand-planter. No time for plowing—the window is too tight, and anyway the straw helps keep moisture. For maize I buy hybrid seed every year—you can't save it. It's about 55 yuan per mu this year. I put down compound fertilizer at planting, about 35 kg per mu, and then at the trumpet stage around late July I'll topdress 15 kg of urea per mu if the rains have been decent. If it's too dry, the fertilizer just sits there and I've burned money. Maize needs less fuss than wheat. Two irrigations: one at jointing, one at tasseling in August. If it's a wet summer like two years ago, maybe only once.

I expect about 400 kg per mu of wheat and 450 kg per mu of maize. That's not the highest in the village, but with 5 mu, stable yields mean my family has flour and some corn to sell. I'm too old to chase records. My job is to make sure we don't have a disaster.
